title: Faults and Quality
description: How to tell a faulty wine from one you simply don't like, and how to judge quality without bias.
L: Explain what to do with a corked bottle

A corked wine smells of damp cardboard, wet dog or a musty cellar. In mild cases, it simply mutes the fruit, making the wine seem dull and flat. The cause is 2,4,6-trichloroanisole, or TCA. Humans can detect it at just a few parts per trillion.

TCA forms when fungi meet chlorine compounds, often in cork bark, but also in barrels, wooden beams or cardboard in wineries. Natural cork producers have cut taint rates by new cleaning methods and screening each cork. A whole winery can be contaminated, affecting wines under any closure.
TCA gives the musty smell. It can be detected in tiny amounts.

A corked wine isn't dangerous, just disappointing. In a restaurant or shop, it's normal to ask for a replacement. Smell first; don't judge by the cork itself, which can smell fine even when the wine doesn't.
Only wines sealed with natural cork can suffer from TCA.
Not true. TCA can contaminate a whole winery through barrels or wood, so wines under screw cap can be affected too, though much more rarely.
Cork taint smells of damp cardboard and mutes fruit
TCA forms from fungi and chlorine compounds
It's harmless but a reason to replace the bottle

An oxidised wine has lost its fresh fruit, smelling of bruised apple, sherry or nuts, with browning colour. It comes from too much contact with oxygen, through a faulty closure, poor storage or careless winemaking. It's a fault in a fresh white, but a deliberate style in Oloroso or tawny Port. Acetaldehyde is the main compound.

Reduction is the opposite: too little oxygen, in a wine with sulphur compounds. It smells of rotten egg, struck match, rubber or cabbage. Hydrogen sulphide, the rotten egg smell, forms when stressed yeast lacks nutrients. Light reduction, struck match, can add complexity in some whites; strong reduction is a fault.
Match each smell to its cause.
Each fault has a typical smell.

Some reduction can be fixed by air: decanting or swirling may blow off struck match or rubber. Persistent rotten egg can sometimes be cleared by a clean copper coin, which binds sulphides. Oxidation can't be undone. Screw caps, which let in little oxygen, can sometimes favour reduction; corks can favour oxidation.
Air can help reduction, not oxidation
Which could be signs of oxidation in a young white?
Fresh lime and green apple are signs of a sound, youthful white.
Oxidation brings bruised apple, browning and loss of fruit
Reduction brings rotten egg, rubber or struck match
Air can fix mild reduction; oxidation is permanent
Explain when each is a fault

Brettanomyces is a yeast that can grow in wine, especially in barrels and in reds with higher pH and low SO2. It produces 4-ethylphenol and 4-ethylguaiacol, smelling of barnyard, sticking plaster, sweat and smoked meat. In small amounts, some tasters find it adds complexity; at higher levels, it masks fruit.

Volatile acidity, VA, is mainly acetic acid, made by acetic bacteria when wine meets air, or by stressed yeast. It smells of vinegar and often comes with ethyl acetate, smelling of nail polish remover. Small amounts lift aromas; too much is a fault. EU limits are about 1.2 g/l for reds and 1.08 g/l for whites, higher for sweet wines.
Which smell is typical of volatile acidity?
Acetic acid and ethyl acetate give vinegar and solvent aromas.

The line between fault and character depends on level and context. Some famous wines, like older Châteauneuf-du-Pape, show a touch of Brett; some great sweet wines have higher VA. A fault is when the compound dominates and hides fruit and place. Personal sensitivity varies a lot.
A small amount of volatile acidity can lift a wine's aromas.
Yes. At low levels VA can add lift; it becomes a fault when vinegar dominates.
Brett gives barnyard and plaster notes, mainly in reds
Volatile acidity smells of vinegar and nail polish
Level and context decide whether it's a fault or character

A wine stored too warm, or left in a hot car, can taste cooked: stewed, jammy fruit, flat and dull. The cork may push out or wine may leak around it. The damage is permanent. Even a few hours above 30 degrees can harm a delicate wine.

Light strike happens when light, especially ultraviolet, reacts with riboflavin and amino acids in wine, creating sulphur compounds that smell of cabbage or wet wool. Clear glass offers no protection; Champagne in clear bottles is especially at risk. Refermentation, when yeast restarts in a bottle with sugar, gives unwanted fizz and cloudiness.
Why are clear glass bottles risky for wine?
They let in light that can cause light strike
Clear glass doesn't filter ultraviolet light, which can create cabbage-like sulphur compounds.

Some things look alarming but are harmless: tartrate crystals, called wine diamonds; sediment in old reds or vintage Port; a slight haze in unfiltered wines; small bubbles in young whites bottled with some carbon dioxide on purpose. Learning these prevents rejecting good bottles.
Which are harmless rather than faults?
Light strike and heat damage are real faults.
Heat damage gives cooked fruit and pushed corks
Light strike gives cabbage smells; refermentation gives fizz
Crystals, sediment and slight haze are harmless

You may dislike a perfectly made wine, or love a simple one. Quality judgement asks whether the wine is well made and expressive of its style and origin. Preference asks whether you enjoy it. Professionals separate the two: a great Fino can be outstanding even for someone who prefers fruity reds.
Quality is not the same as liking

Use balance, length, intensity and complexity, plus typicity: does it taste like its grape and place? Bias creeps in through price, label, reputation, glass colour and even music. In blind tests, wine experts have rated the same wine differently when told it was expensive. Tasting blind removes much of this.
Match each bias to its source.
Biases are natural; tasting blind and in a fixed order reduce them.
Taste the same wine twice in a flight without knowing. If your notes differ a lot, you've just measured your own consistency, a humbling and useful exercise.
What is the best way to reduce label and price bias?
Taste only one wine at a time
Tasting blind removes the influence of label, price and reputation.
Quality and personal preference are different questions
Judge with balance, length, intensity, complexity and typicity
Blind tasting reduces price and label bias
Match each fault to its typical smell.
What causes hydrogen sulphide in wine?
Yeast short of nitrogen produces rotten egg smells.
Tartrate crystals in a white wine are a fault.
Not true. They're harmless salts of tartaric acid.
Which help reduce bias when judging quality?
Cork taint is caused by the compound ____.
TCA, oxidation, reduction, Brett and VA are the main faults
Heat and light damage come from poor storage
Level and context decide fault or character
Quality is judged with criteria, ideally blind
